div.l: Sing, goddess, the godlike wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus,
that sociopathic wrath that caused countless sufferings for the Achaeans.
of warriors. And it began to make their bodies into picked-over scraps for dogs
and for birds, all of them; and the plan of Zeus began to be fulfilled,
from the point where truly first, the two having both begun a competition with each other, both of them faced off,
the son of Atreus, lord of men, and god-like Achilles.
Who then of the gods threw together the two of them to fight in competition with one another?
The son of Leto and of Zeus: for that one, filled with anger at the king,
set in motion an evil sickness up through the camp. And the soldiers began to be killed,
because he showed disrespect to that man Chryses, the god-talker.
What man? -- the son of Atreus. Here is what happened: that man, came to the swift ships of the Achaeans
both in order to free his daughter and bearing boundless ransom,
high up on his golden staff. And he began to plead with all the Achaeans,
and especially with the two sons of Atreus, the organizers of the soldiers:
“Sons of Atreus and also all other well-greaved Achaeans,
with my blessing may the gods, having homes on Olympus, give as a gift to you
to destroy and pillage the city of Priam, and to return homewards well;
but for me free my beloved child, and accept this ransom,
showing reverence for the son of Zeus, the far-shooter Apollo.”
At that point indeed all the Achaeans shouted their approval,
both to treat with decency the sacrifice-leader and to accept the shining ransom;
However, this was not sweet to Atreus’ son, Agamemnon, in his heart,
Instead, he dismissed him cruelly. And he began to impose upon him a harsh command:
“(emphasizing with tone and body language the pronoun “I”) I, on my part, may not come upon you, old man, near the hollow ships,
either hanging around now or coming back later,
lest even at that time the staff and wreaths of the god may not protect you.
And that woman I, for my part, will not free, until (with emphasis) old age comes upon her
in our house in Argos, far from her fatherland,
working the loom and serving my very own bed.
Instead go away! Do not keep provoking me me thus so that you might make your way home more safely than if you remain.”
So he spoke. [δ'] That old man became frightened. And he began to obey the command.
But he walked in silence to the shore of the loudly-roaring sea.
And then, going far away, that old man began speaking as god-talker
to lord Apollo, he whom light-haired Leto bore:
“Hear me, silver-bowed one, who have taken under your protection Chrysa
and sacred Cilla, and are lord of Tenedos by force,
Smintheus, if at any time I roofed over a shrine pleasing to you,
or if indeed at any time I completely burned fat thigh-bones for you,
of bulls and of goats, but fulfill this desire for me:
may the Danaans pay their respects for my own tears with your arrows.”
So he spoke praying. Phoebus Apollo listened to that man [δ'].
Seething with anger in his heart, he came down from the top of Olympus,
carrying his bow and his covered quiver on his shoulders.
And the arrows rattled noisily on the shoulders of the god as he seethed with anger,
once he himself began to move. Then [δ'] that one made his way like night.
Then he began to crouch far away from the ships. [δ'] He fired an arrow in their midst-
Fearsome grew the rattle from the silver bow.
First he began to go after the mules and the swift dogs,
but then, letting fly a sharp arrow against the men themselves,
he began to strike home. The pyres of the corpses, one after another, were kept burning without any break.
For nine days, to start with, the arrows of the god kept moving up through the camp,
On that tenth day, however, Achilles summoned the soldiers to an assembly,
The white-armed goddess Hera, as it happened, placed this within that man’s mind.
This was the reason: she kept worrying about the Danaans, because [ῥα] she kept watching them as they died.
And as for those men, after they became gathered together and so were assembled,
swift-footed Achilles, standing up, spoke among them [δ']:
“Son of Atreus, now I believe that we us, having been driven back,
will return to our homes again, if we possibly might flee death, at any rate.
If truly war and plague together will force the Achaeans into submission.
Instead, come, [δή] let us speak to either some seer or sacrifice-leader,
or even a dream-interpreter, for a dream is also from Zeus.
That man may say why Phoebus Apollo became so greatly filled with anger;
whether [ἄρ'] that one is showing his dissatisfaction at a vow or at a hecatomb,
or if he in any way, having met with the rich aroma of sheep suited for this purpose and goats,
possibly would be willing to avert destruction from us.”
And so, having spoken in this way, that man began to sit down. And among them stood up
Calchas, son of Thestor, best by far of bird-interpreters,
who knew the things that are, and the things that will be, and the things that were before.
through his own gift of foresight, which Phoebus Apollo furnished to him.
That man, thinking benevolently for them, addressed the assembly, and spoke in their midst:
“Achilles, dear to Zeus, you order me to give an account of
the wrath of Apollo, the lord far-shooter:
therefore I will be the one who will speak. And as for you, take this in and swear to me
most decidedly to help me with determination, with your words and with your hands.
holds power over all the Argives, and whom the Achaeans obey:
for the king has more power, whenever he is angry at an inferior man.
Here’s the reason: even if, in fact, he would choke down his anger on that one particular day,
nevertheless just as certainly going forward he holds a grudge in his chest, until he can fulfill it,
So, as for you, make yourself clear, if you will protect me.”
Swift-footed Achilles, answering, addressed that man:
“Having taken heart fully, give voice to the god’s message, whatever [τι] it [0] you know.
For by Apollo, beloved of Zeus, and for whom you, Calchas,
speaking with authority, reveal divine messages to the Danaans,
no [τις] one, while I am alive and while I am able to see upon this earth,
will bear against you heavy hands near the hollow ships-
not any of all the Danaans together, not even if you are speaking about Agamemnon,
he who claims to be by far the best of the Achaeans.”
And then, you could see, he took courage and he began to speak, the blameless prophet:
“Truely [γ'], that one finds fault neither with a vow nor a hecatomb,
but rather, because of the god-talker, the man to whom Agamemnon showed disrespect:
he did not [δ'] free his daughter, nor did he accept the ransom.
[ἄρ'] Because of this the far-shooter gave sufferings and he will continue to give still.
That one [γε] certainly will not [δ'] first drive off shameful destruction for the Danaans,
without a price, without a ransom, and lead a sacred hecatomb
into Chrysa: then we, having appeased him, might cause a change of heart.”
And so[γ'], that man, having spoken thus, began to sit down : Then among them stood up
the warrior son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
stricken with pain. His black heart completely
began being filled with rage. [δέ] His two eyes became like blazing fire.
Glaring evilly first of all , he addressed Calchas:
“Seer of evil things, you have not yet once said a favorable thing to me:
these evil things are always dear to you in your heart to prophesy,
and as for the fortunate, you have neither yet spoken any word nor accomplished anything.
And now, speaking on behalf of the gods, you declare among the Danaans
that the far-shooter produces sufferings for them because of this particular thing :
because I, for my part, was not willing to accept the shining ransom of the girl Chryseis
, since I very much wish to hold that woman
at home. And, as it happens, in fact I have come to prefer her over Clytemnestra,
my lawful wife, since she is not inferior to her,
not in form, and not in stature, and not, to be honest ,in mind, nor in any respect in the things that she can produce.
Yet even so I am willing to give her back, if this really is better:
I, for my part, wish the soldiers to be safe, rather than to be wiped out.
As for me, prepare a prize appropriate for my rank immediately, so that alone
of the Argives I am not without a prize, since this is also not fitting.
After all, each and every one of you see this, don’t you- that my prize goes elsewhere.”
And then swift-footed godly Achilles proceeded to answer him:
“Son of Atreus, the man with the most glory, and most attached to possessions of all,
how exactly will the Achaeans, great-spirited, give you a prize?
We do not [δέ] know of many common stores set aside anywhere at all.
Rather, as we all know, the things which we destroyed and pillaged from the cities, these things have been divided up.
and on the other hand it is also not fitting for the soldiers to gather together again these clawed-back things.
Instead, you for your part now release this girl to the god. On our part, the Achaeans
will repay you three times, and even four times, over, if Zeus at some point
may confer the gift to sack completely the well-walled city Troy.”
And answering, the ruler Agamemnon addressed that man:
“Do not in this way, although being skillful, godlike Achilles,
keep cheating with your mind, since you will not slip past nor persuade me.
Do you really want, while you yourself are to hold onto your own prize, me, for my part, like this
to sit still lacking? Are you telling me to give back this particular woman?
[ἀλλ'] Mind you, if the great-spirited Achaeans will give me a prize,

having fashioned it exactly according to my heart, so that it will be worth just as much … (Agamemnon uses non-verbal communication -- perhaps a shrug of the shoulders -- to communicate that this would be acceptable)
But, if they should not make a gift, then I myself, going in person would seize for myself
either your prize or that of Ajax, or that of Odysseus.
Having taken possession, I will lead it away. That man [δέ] would become angry and stay angry, whomever I would approach.
Nevertheless, that being said , certainly we will return to consider once again these things,
Now, come. Let us drag a black ship into the divine sea.
Let us gather within sufficient rowers. A hecatomb
let us place inside. The beautiful-cheeked Chryseis herself
we will cause to go on board . And let some single counsel-bearing man be the leader,
either Ajax or Idomeneus or godlike Odysseus,
or you, Son of Peleus, most aggressive of all men,
until, having performed sacrifices, you will appease him, the far-shooter.”
Having given a dark look [ἄρ'] swift-footed Achilles addressed that man:
“How dare you! You, all clothed in indecency, obsessed by profit,
how would any of the Achaeans with a ready mind listen to your words,
either to go on a journey or with his own strength to fight with men?
The fact of the matter is: I certainly did not come on account of Trojan spearmen
here in order to fight, since they are not at fault to me in any way:
for they did not ever drive away my own cattle, nor [μὲν] my horses,
and not in warrior-nourishing, fertile Phthia did they ever
harm the harvest, since there are many things between:
many [τε] shady mountains and also the roaring sea.
Instead you, oh massively indecent one, together we followed so that you might be pleased,
seeking to gain respect for Menelaus and for yourself, dog-face,
from the Trojans. Of these things you do not consider at all. Nor do you give a damn.
And now you make threats that you yourself to seize for yourself my prize,
for which I struggled at length, and which the sons of the Achaeans gave to me.
Certainly I do not ever have a prize equal to yours, whenever the Achaeans
destroy and pillage a well-managed city of the Trojans.
Instead, you may be sure, the greater part of the miserable fighting
my own hands perform; nevertheless if and when the division of spoils is at hand,
for you the prize is much greater, while a smaller yet precious prize I, for my part,
go on my way carrying to the ships, after I am exhausted from waging war.
But now I will go to Phthia, since it is surely much superior
to go home with the curved ships. With me being disrespected here here, I do not plan,
in the future to ladle out riches and wealth for you.”
And then the lord of men, Agamemnon, began to answer him:
“By all means run away, if your heart is stirred in that direction. [δέ] I myself certainly do not
plead with you to stay on account of me: beside me, you can be sure, are [0] others as well
who would respect me -- and most of all, Zeus, the giver of counsel.
You are the most hateful [δέ] to me of the kings fostered by Zeus:
for competing with others is always dear to you, as [0] are both wars and battles.
If you are very strong, at some point a god gave this [γ'] to you.
Going home with both your own ships and with your own comrades,
lord it over the Myrmidons. [δ'] And as for me, I don’t give a damn about you,
nor do I worry about you bearing a grudge. But I will make the following threat to you:
as Phoebus Apollo is taking away for himself from me Chryseis,
that woman, you can be sure, I myself will send on her away with both my own ship and my own comrades.
For my part, however, I would lead beautiful-cheeked Briseis,
that prize of yours, going myself to your resting-place, so that you may clearly see
how greatly I am superior to you, and another man as well will fear
to declare himself equal to me, and to treat himself as a peer to my face.”
So he spoke. And pain materialized in the son of Peleus. The heart
in his hairy chest was torn in two directions:
whether he himself, for his part, having drawn for himself the sharp sword from beside his thigh,
would first make those men stand back while he for his part would kill the son of Atreus,
or whether he could put a stop to his anger and restrain his heart.
As he was turning over these things through his thoughts and through his heart,
he was beginning to draw for himself [δ'] out of its sheath sheath a great sword, but Athena came
from heaven. The reason for this was that the white-armed goddess Hera sent her forth,
both caring about and concerned for the two men equally in her heart.
She stood [δ'] behind him, and by his light hair she gripped the son of Peleus,
making herself visible to him alone. Not anyone of the others [δ'] could himself see.
Achilles felt astonishment [δ'], and turned himself around. And right then and there he recognized
Pallas Athena. and her two eyes appeared fearsome.
[καί] Having addressed her, he began to give voice to winged words:
“There you are! Why, daughter of aegis-holding Zeus, have you come?
Is it so that you might see for yourself the outrageous behavior of Agamemnon, son of Atreus?
Whatever the answer I will speak to you openly. And this as well I expect to be fulfilled:
by his outrageous actions soon he is likely to destroy his life.”
Then to him the goddess spoke, silvery-eyed Athena:
“I, for my part, came in order to put a stop to this rage of yours -- if you [κε] might obey --
down from the heavens. The white-armed goddess Hera sent me forth,
both caring about and concerned for both equally int her heart.
Instead, come on. Step away from this quarrel. Do not keep drawing for yourself the sword in your hand.
Instead, by all means, with words as much as you please paint him a nasty picture of how he can be sure it will be:
Because I will tell you outright how this is is. And as well this will in reality be fulfilled.
In the future, there will be present in your possession three times as many shining gifts
because of the outrageous behavior that we see here. As for you, hold yourself back. Listen to us.”
And , replying, swift-footed Achilles said to her:
“Of course, goddess, it is necessary to heed a statement from the two of you,
even though really filled up with anger in one’s heart. For it is better this way.
Whoever would obey the gods, they really [τ'] listen to him.”
He spoke. And on the silver hilt he held his heavy hand,
Back into the sheath he shoved the great sword, and he did not disobey
the command of Athena. But as for that goddess, she had already departed to Olympus,
into the home of aegis-holding Zeus among the other divinities.
The son of Peleus [δ'] yet again with harsh words
spoke to the son of Atreus. And he was not yet leaving off from his anger;
“Swollen with wine, having the eyes of a dog but the heart of a deer,
not ever to arm yourself for battle together with the army,
nor ever to enter an ambush [δ'] with the most outstanding of the Achaeans
have you had the fortitude in your heart. That seems to you to be death.
to take away for yourself gifts from whoever may have speak against you.
You are a king who devours his people, because you lord over nobodies!
For truly, son of Atreus, you would now have acted abusively for the last time.
Instead I will say out loud to you, and besides I will swear a great oath.
Truly by this very staff, which not ever in truth will sprout leaves and branches,
after it first left behind its stump in the mountains,
nor will it flourish again. For the bronze stripped it all around
both the leaves and the bark. Now, however, the sons of the Achaeans,
acting as judges, carry it in their palms, they who
[τε] defend the laws of the cosmos on behalf of Zeus. This [δέ] will be a great oath to you.
each and every one of them! And then you, though stricken with pain, will not have the power
to provide protection in the least, when ever many fall dying at the hands of Hector the man-slaughterer.
You [δ'] will gouge open your own heart within,
consumed with fury because you in no way showed respect to the best of the Achaeans.”
So spoke the son of Peleus. And he flung against the ground the staff,
drilled with golden studs. And he himself began to sit.
And the son of Atreus from the other side continued in wrath. And among them Nestor,
pleasing in speech lept up, the articulate assembly-speaker of the Pylians,
and from that man’s tongue speech began to flow, sweeter than honey.
